cathedrals.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral, New York
cathedrals.love: 1. The livestream page is digital hospitality at its best: daily readings linked to the USCCB site, archived Masses by liturgical title, a Mass Collection giving link, and a dial-in phone Mass — — for people with no internet at all. Someone thought about the grandmother without Wi-Fi, and that matters. | 2. The FAQ page is the finest visitor document in this pilot so far: it answers questions people are almost embarrassed to ask (luggage, dogs, holy water, ticket rules) with practical grace, names real humans to call, and even tells you which Masses have music. | 3. Marquee events get real storytelling, not bare listings — the Guardian's Mass, the Napa Institute's Eucharistic procession through Midtown, and LUMINISCENCE (with proceeds named for the Kilgen organ campaign) each get dedicated, shareable pages with images and named participants.
cathedrals.opp: 1. The OCIA/becoming-Catholic path is invisible. A cathedral that draws five million annual visitors and streams Mass worldwide is perfectly positioned for an 'Interested in becoming Catholic?' doorway — a named coordinator and a one-page start-here would turn tourist curiosity into discipleship. | 2. Giving is generous but scattered: the Mass Collection link (Blackbaud) lives on the livestream page while Friends of Music and restoration giving live elsewhere. A single 'Support the Cathedral' hub naming where each dollar goes would turn fragmented generosity into a confident ask. | 3. The FAQ deserves a bigger stage — it doubles as the newcomer desk today. Promoting it as 'Plan Your Visit' with parking/transit, a kids welcome, and the becoming-Catholic doorway would complete the newcomer journey.
dims: Genuinely invitational. The homepage opens with a human story (an interview with Antonia Acutis), the livestream page greets remote viewers with daily readings, a phone-in Mass option, and a virtual candle, and the Rector's public words are 'we want all to feel at home and welcome.' It reads as a front porch, not a bulletin board.

Both, but newcomer-weighted: the cathedral explicitly serves 'five million annual visitors' and tourists, so most pages (FAQ, tours, livestream) speak to first-time visitors as much as to regular worshippers.

More featured than listed. The events feed carries descriptions and images for special moments, the choir has a proud narrative page, press releases tell real stories (papal busts, relic pilgrimages), and the concert programs name every soloist. Daily Masses are plain listings, which is appropriate.

Not found. The FAQ — otherwise one of the best newcomer documents in this pilot — has no 'How do I become Catholic?' path, no OCIA/RCIA mention, and no named coordinator. A cathedral with the world's attention should make the door into the Church as visible as the door into the building.

Scattered but human: baptisms and weddings run through a named coordinator (Grace Baldizon, [email protected]), Mass cards have a dedicated page (with the striking detail that intentions are booked over a year out — the 2028 schedule opens February 2027), and communion guidance appears in the worship aids. No single sacraments landing page was found.

Yes — a genuine FAQ page (saintpatrickscathedral.org/faqs), built for visitors not insiders. Gloriam questions scored: Communion eligibility (1 — covered in the Order of Worship PDF's pastoral communion guidance), 'what should I wear'-adjacent conduct rules (0.5), who to ask for help (0.5 — tour/dev emails, no greeter named). Not covered: bathrooms/changing tables, becoming Catholic, cry room/children, 'what if I don't know what I'm doing.' Rough score: ~2 of 7.

Excellent. Full Mass and confession schedule on the FAQ page (Mon–Fri six daily Masses; Saturday vigil; eight Sunday Masses including a 4:00 PM Spanish Mass), echoed on the homepage metadata, the livestream page, and a one-tap dial-in option. 'Which Masses have music?' is even answered — a lovely touch for visitors choosing their experience. cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels
cathedrals.love: The events calendar is a model of hospitality: every event — from the 44th annual Red Mass to Simbang Gabi's Parade of Parols — gets its own richly written, shareable page that explains the tradition for outsiders instead of assuming insider knowledge. That is evangelization-minded web writing, and it's rare. | Sunday Mass times live right on the homepage — English and Spanish, weekdays and weekends, plus confession and adoration hours — exactly where a first-time visitor needs them, with zero clicks required. The essentials are treated as essentials. | Seasonal content is planned months ahead (a full Lent 2026 program page with dates and Holy Week schedule; Christmas events promoted in October), and the Spanish-speaking community is served as a first-class audience — bilingual Masses, Spanish news posts, El Coro de la Catedral. This site knows who walks through its doors.
cathedrals.opp: A single 'Sacraments' hub would be a gift to newcomers: baptism, wedding, funeral, and anointing information currently lives in different places (and wedding guidance still points to writing the pastor, per an older bulletin). One warm page — 'Celebrate a sacrament at the Cathedral' — with a named contact for each would close the loop. | The OCIA and Adult Confirmation invitations are admirably prominent; adding a named contact person and a simple 'what happens next' outline would turn interest into action, especially for adults who may feel nervous about taking the first step. | The livestream is a genuine ministry to homebound Catholics well beyond Los Angeles (TV, radio, and online). A small 'Watch' hub — one page with the stream schedule and how to tune in on each platform — would make it findable, and it would be the perfect home for the warm, people-centered stories the site's news stream is ready to tell more of.
dims: Mixed: institutional flagship framing with warm, invitational event copy. The homepage opens with a 'Year of St. Francis' campaign carousel, then a mission statement that positions the Cathedral as serving 'the total Archdiocese of over 5 million Catholics' and 'the heart of all 287 Parish Churches and communities' — appropriate for a metropolitan cathedral, but written for insiders and visitors rather than addressed to a newcomer personally. Individual event teasers, however, use genuinely invitational language: 'Everyone is welcome,' 'Join us,' 'We invite you.' There is no pastor video greeting or 'new here' path visible via text fetch, so it reads as a welcoming bulletin board for the archdiocesan family rather than a personal invitation to a stranger.

Both, leaning toward current Catholics plus cultural visitors. Content serves the archdiocesan faithful (Red Mass for legal professionals, Transitional Diaconate Ordination, archdiocesan liturgies) and tourists/architecture visitors (the 'Interior' page is essentially a guided tour of the building's theology; free daily tours are offered). Newcomer signals exist but are secondary: an Adult Confirmation invitation and OCIA interest form are promoted on the homepage and news stream.

Featured, not listed. Events carry rich descriptions with cultural and historical context (the Red Mass tradition traced to the 11th century; the 117 Vietnamese martyrs canonized by John Paul II in 1988; Simbang Gabi explained as one of the oldest Filipino Christmas traditions). The Volunteers/ministries page gives each ministry a theology-rich paragraph (hospitality, altar server, lector, music, sacristan) rather than a bare directory. This is storytelling-first promotion, done well.

Prominent but contact-light. 'Adult Confirmation Registration Now Open!' is promoted on both the homepage and news stream ('Are you a baptized Catholic adult who has received First Communion but has not yet received the Sacrament of Confirmation? The Cathedral invites adults seeking Confirmation to join our Adult Confirmation preparation program.'). The news stream also references an OCIA Interest Form with an August 7 deadline. However, no currently named OCIA contact appears in 2026 content via text fetch (a 2023 news item named Deacon Ricardo Mora; the volunteer coordinator contact shown is for volunteering, not OCIA). Path is one click from the homepage via the promo, but the human to call is not visible.

Scattered — no unified sacraments hub page found. Reconciliation hours are embedded on the homepage; Mass Intentions has its own dedicated page with suggested stipends ($10 weekday / $20 Sunday); weddings and baptisms require contacting the Cathedral Pastor in writing (per an older bulletin reference); anointing of the sick, Mass cards, and funerals are handled via the parish office at. Each piece exists, but a newcomer seeking 'how do I get married here' or 'how do I baptize my child' must assemble the path themselves.

N. No dedicated FAQ page found via text fetch. Score on Gloriam's 7 questions: 0 — none of the seven (bathrooms/changing tables, what to wear, who to ask for help, how to become Catholic, cry room/children, 'what if I don't know what I'm doing,' Communion eligibility) are addressed in a single FAQ. Practical visitor information (free tours daily at 1pm, parking validation, cafe and gift shop hours, closures) is instead woven into event details and news posts — accurate, but scattered.

Excellent — among the best possible placements. The full Sunday schedule (8:00 AM English, 10:00 AM English, 12:30 PM Spanish) and weekday schedule (Mon–Fri 7:00 AM and 12:10 PM English) appear directly on the homepage with zero clicks required. Confession times (M W F 11:00 AM–12:00 PM) and Friday Eucharistic Adoration (7:30 AM–12:00 PM, Blessed Sacrament Chapel) sit in the same homepage block. No dedicated Mass-times page was found, but none is needed when the information is this visible. Live-browser check 2026-10-28: Mass times are shown on the homepage itself.

Strong and specific. Homepage lists confessions M/W/F 11:00 AM–12:00 PM; an older bulletin reference lists reconciliation Mon–Fri 11am–12pm; the seasonal Lent page expands penance services to M/W/F during Lent plus a Wednesday Holy Hour after the 12:10pm Mass. Friday adoration in the Blessed Sacrament Chapel is on the homepage. Confession is treated as a headline ministry, not a footnote.

Clear and multi-layered, on the professional OSV Hub platform (osvhub.com). The homepage carries a direct 'Donate' appeal that honestly frames the need ('The Cathedral is not funded by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles and depends on the generosity and good will of the people'). A dedicated 'Ways to Give' page (olacathedral.org/give) adds Cathedral Associates, Paving Stones, Tribute & Memorial Gifts, and a Legacy Society. Online giving platform named: OSV (Our Sunday Visitor) Hub. Live-browser check 2026-10-28: OSV Hub.

Strong. Phone appears in the footer of every page. Named humans with direct lines and emails appear on ministry pages: Cari Hilger, Volunteer Coordinator,; outreach office at, (rent/utilities assistance); mausoleum line; gift shop. Address and office hours were found via third-party references, not rendered on the site itself in text fetch. Overall: a real person is reachable with minimal effort.

The traditional PDF bulletin is stale — the only ecatholic-hosted bulletin found is dated March 2020 (pre-pandemic). But the 'News' stream functions as the living bulletin and is fresh: items dated October 2026 (CicLAvia traffic advisory Oct 11, Dia de los Muertos altar, OCIA deadline) with an archive stretching back years. The parish has effectively migrated bulletin-style communication into dated, shareable news posts — the 2020 PDF is simply a legacy artifact that could be removed.

High — this is a strength. Rather than PDF dumps, announcements live as individual news posts and each event has a dedicated shareable page with its own URL (olacathedral.org/events/red-mass, /vietnamese-martyrs-mass, /veterans-day-mass, /thanksgiving-day-mass, /simbang-gabi). The seasonal Lent and All Souls landing pages work the same way. Everything is a permalinkable page, not a scanned page.

Active, current, and genuinely used. Twelve events listed October through December 2026, each described in full sentences with cultural context, times, locations, parking details ($12 for the theater performance; validated parking for Mass), and ticket links (Eventbrite, lamasterchorale.org, latinotheaterco.org). The calendar reads as a curated program of archdiocesan life — Red Mass, All Souls Vespers, Vietnamese Martyrs Mass, Transitional Diaconate Ordination, Thanksgiving Mass with food drive, Guadalupe pageant, Simbang Gabi, LA Master Chorale Las Posadas, Messiah concert — not an empty grid.

N. No parish school. The complex includes the Cathedral, mausoleum/crypt, gift shop, Galero Grill cafe (operated by Levy Restaurants), conference center, and Cathedral Center archdiocesan offices — but no school to flag for the schools vertical.

Strong seasonal faith content, published ahead of the season. A dedicated Lent 2026 landing page (olacathedral.org/lent) lays out the full Lenten program — penance services, Wednesday Holy Hour dates, Stations of the Cross dates, Holy Week schedule PDF, parking validation — with real catechesis ('During Lent, we seek the Lord in prayer by reading Sacred Scripture; we serve by giving alms; and we practice self-control through fasting'). An All Souls page (olacathedral.org/all-souls) supports the November remembrance season, and the homepage carousel leads with a 'Year of St. Francis' campaign. Christmas-season programming (Las Posadas, Simbang Gabi, Guadalupe play) was already listed in October.

Partial. We expect this to be resolved within a few days') confirms the stream is a real, maintained ministry. Yes — flagship events get dedicated, shareable pages, not bulletin-only mentions. Each has a unique URL, a named graphic, and a multi-paragraph description. The events index page itself is a rich editorial calendar.

Partial. Partial. Partial and announcement-leaning. The hero of the site's imagery is the building itself (the Interior page celebrates architecture and light). Faces and people-stories are the missing layer.

Real, local, professional cathedral photography (the COLA_LA photo series, 2026-dated event graphics, per-event artwork). The visual emphasis is the building — alabaster windows, nave, organ — which is fitting for a landmark cathedral and a visitor audience. Studio 33 A.D. is the standout ministry in this batch: a parish-run media studio (est. 2020) streaming Sunday Masses, posting weekly homilies, featuring ministries, and even livestreaming weddings and funerals — digital hospitality with a brand and a mission. | 2. The site has a human pulse: a homepage prayer request for staffer Joe Wilson after his accident, 2026 parish picnic photos, named staff with direct emails. This reads like a family, not an institution.

The parish clearly has highlights (the 2026 parish picnic photos are right there); the captions just haven't caught up. | 2. Name the OCIA human. The 'Becoming Catholic' page lays out the journey beautifully ('Easy to start: 1. Contact Us...') but step 1 doesn't name who to contact — a coordinator name, email, and photo would turn interest into action. | 3. Add a 'Plan Your Visit' companion to the tour hours.
